blocks.text: Quick verdict

ProxyEmpire is the better value for small and mid-size teams: entry traffic costs $3.50/GB against Bright Data's $8/GB list price, prepaid gigabytes never expire, and ISP targeting is free. Bright Data is the better choice for hardened targets and enterprise pipelines, where its larger pool, ZIP and carrier targeting, Web Unlocker, SERP API and Scraping Browser reduce engineering effort, and for Google-heavy SERP work where ProxyEmpire was weakest in independent tests. Check for Bright Data's frequent half-price promotions before deciding.

Bright Data and ProxyEmpire both sell residential, mobile, ISP and datacenter proxies, but at very different price points and levels of sophistication. Bright Data is the enterprise default, with a 150M+ pool, ZIP and ASN targeting and managed unblocking, SERP and browser products. ProxyEmpire is a value-focused network where prepaid traffic never expires, ISP targeting is free and a $1.97 trial covers residential and mobile. This comparison shows when Bright Data's premium is justified.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire sells residential, mobile, static residential and datacenter proxies from one dashboard and competes on flexibility. Traffic you prepay never expires, ISP-level targeting is free, and the $1.97 trial lets you test both residential and mobile networks before committing. Its 30M+ advertised pool is smaller on paper than the enterprise providers, but independent testing has rated its real reachable pool well relative to its claims.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: Bright Data vs ProxyEmpire

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

At 10 GB a month, ProxyEmpire is the cheaper option at about $35 against $80 for Bright Data, roughly 56% less. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; Bright Data comes to about $499. Look past the per-GB figure too. ProxyEmpire lets unused traffic carry forward, while Bright Data's allowance does not (monthly plan allowances reset each cycle). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, Bright Data (150M+) is about 5.0x larger than ProxyEmpire (30M+). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. The limitation on the ProxyEmpire side: stable connections and traffic that never expires.

SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How ProxyEmpire compares: Google was its weakest target in independent tests.

Social media and multi-account management: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions. The limitation on the Bright Data side: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. How ProxyEmpire compares: free city and ISP targeting.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How ProxyEmpire compares: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost.
Tight budgets: ProxyEmpire. ProxyEmpire has the edge here. Why: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and ProxyEmpire before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Bright Data and ProxyEmpire is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, ProxyEmpire in 2, and 0 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
